prompt:
I need the front end for Roostline. A survey workspace for independent wildlife consultants who place acoustic bat detectors across proposed wind energy sites and report which turbine locations pose the most risk.

Who's using it: Dr. Helen Ostrowski, a self-employed bat ecologist with 15 years of fieldwork who runs her own one-person consultancy. A wind developer has hired her for pre-construction surveys on a ridge in central Pennsylvania. She knows bat ecology and call identification deeply and does her own analysis and reporting.

What they're doing right now: The first six-week deployment has just been recovered and processed. Before her draft report goes to the developer and the state wildlife agency next Friday, she needs to work out which of the 38 proposed turbine pads sit within 200 m of stations that recorded high activity. She's paying special attention to two stations on the northeast spur that picked up possible Indiana bat calls, a federally endangered species. She also has to decide where to move eight detectors for the autumn migration deployment. She wants better coverage of the saddle between the two ridgetops and the forest edge near the creek, where she suspects a commuting corridor from the known hibernaculum.

What's in the system at this point: Project 'Burnt Cabin Ridge Wind', a 2,150-acre site with elevation from 1,480 to 2,310 ft. 24 detector stations, each with coordinates, mic height (3 m or 30 m on met towers), habitat type and deployment dates (Jun 1 – Jul 13, 2026). 38 proposed turbine pads with coordinates and hub heights of 105 m, plus access roads and the forest-edge boundary. Nightly call counts per station for 7 species groups (hoary, eastern red, silver-haired, big brown, little brown, tricolored, Myotis sodalis-possible), 41,800 files in total, with 312 still awaiting manual vetting. Two stations, S-17 and S-19, have 14 possible Indiana bat passes. A known hibernaculum sits 4.1 km northeast and two streams cross the site. Nightly wind speed and temperature come from the met tower.

Build it as a working web app, opened in the state that person would see at that moment. No backend: use realistic mock data (no lorem ipsum, no placeholder names), and make the interactive parts actually work client-side.

Use whatever framework and tooling you like. When you're done there must be a static production build in ./out with ./out/index.html as the entry point. It will be served from the root of a plain static file server (no rewrites, no server code) and viewed in a desktop browser at 1440×900.
